title: Freedom and Responsibility
text:
Existentialist philosophers insisted that human beings are not born with a fixed essence; instead, they define themselves through the choices they make. Sartre famously argued that we are 'condemned to be free', since no external authority can relieve us of the burden of deciding. This radical autonomy is precisely what makes existence feel both exhilarating and anguishing. Consequently, the individual cannot evade responsibility by appealing to custom or divine command.

Critics, however, contend that this emphasis on individual choice risks neglecting the social and economic conditions that constrain what options are actually available. A person born into poverty, they argue, does not face the same range of decisions as someone privileged. Defenders of existentialism respond that acknowledging such constraints does not negate freedom, but rather obliges us to act authentically within them. The tension between these views remains one of the most productive debates in modern philosophy.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what do existentialists say defines human beings?
options: A fixed essence present at birth

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what might the emphasis on individual choice neglect?
options: The social and economic conditions that constrain options

questions.text: What can be inferred from Sartre's phrase 'condemned to be free'?
options: Freedom brings a heavy burden of responsibility
Freedom is granted only by authorities
Freedom is limited to the wealthy

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about the defenders of existentialism?
options: They believe constraints do not eliminate freedom but shape how one acts
They deny that social conditions exist
They think authentic action is impossible
They agree that choices depend entirely on birth

the freedom to govern oneself and make one's own choices
making you feel excited and energized

paragraph_translations: Los filósofos existencialistas insistían en que los seres humanos no nacen con una esencia fija; en cambio, se definen a sí mismos mediante las decisiones que toman. Sartre afirmó de forma célebre que estamos 'condenados a ser libres', ya que ninguna autoridad externa puede liberarnos de la carga de decidir. Esta autonomía radical es precisamente lo que hace que la existencia resulte a la vez estimulante y angustiante. En consecuencia, el individuo no puede eludir la responsabilidad apelando a la costumbre o a un mandato divino.

Sin embargo, los críticos sostienen que este énfasis en la elección individual corre el riesgo de descuidar las condiciones sociales y económicas que restringen las opciones realmente disponibles. Una persona nacida en la pobreza, argumentan, no enfrenta la misma gama de decisiones que alguien privilegiado. Los defensores del existencialismo responden que reconocer tales restricciones no niega la libertad, sino que nos obliga a actuar de manera auténtica dentro de ellas. La tensión entre estas posturas sigue siendo uno de los debates más productivos de la filosofía moderna.
